title: The AI Office Hype Hasn't Settled, and the Personal Agent War Has Already Begun | Breaking Down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
dek: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and hasn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal agent hype, capital is grabbing tickets more than responding to real demand.
why: Four frontline product people break down four paths — Town, Instinct, Grok Bot, Muse — and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. Information density is high, but the second half is worth more.
who: Product managers, investors and engineers watching AI application-layer startups, especially those building or preparing to build personal assistant products and needing to judge this round's valuation and product cadence.
skip: The 01:31 to 01:45 segment with a North American junior-year founder is mostly fundraising narrative, with information density clearly lower than the surrounding sections.

points.body: Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still had fewer than 100,000 users, yet its valuation rose from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month market rumors of a new round have already reached $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old unknown with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan put it bluntly: what capital is buying is not the entrepreneur or the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it can grab a ticket at the price of the next-generation personal operating system.

points.h: The line between tool and person is initiative
points.body: The biggest difference between this wave of agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. There are two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs context re-explained every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are like a friend or colleague; second, initiative — in Manus, setting up automated tasks still depends on prompts, on you spelling out rules and intent, and that is not initiative. True initiative is subjective agency — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and proactively comes over to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

points.h: Office agents organize by project, personal agents organize by person
points.body: The core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along a mission or project dimension, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centered on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences, and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can co-drive. In personal scenarios, model capability and the harness layer matter less, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks; office agents care a lot about task completion rate.

points.h: Town first trades email for the user's delegation right
points.body: The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile app, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC, and it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you frequently send and receive, automatically archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you confirm. It goes deeper in the email scenario than any other agent, and has already achieved fairly viral spread overseas, especially in school-related scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and bit by bit acquire the user's ultimate delegation right.

points.h: Poke didn't take off not because of technical limits
points.body: Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make standalone apps, but Poke didn't take off. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could have done it completely at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-delegation route, able to access credit cards, screen, microphone, book flights, buy things — things users hadn't seen, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content recommendation accuracy, taking the proactive push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it didn't do the step of "finishing things for you."

points.h: Cloud agents must handle three environments
points.body: Mark says building a cloud agent was a painful lesson: local agents and cloud agents are completely different things. To build personal AI you need it available anytime, anywhere — you can't lose contact just because you close your laptop screen. The cloud must handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context transfer between these three environments are extremely complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably on the cloud took at least two months; excluding detours, polishing a sincere work takes at least three to four months.

points.h: Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two different businesses
points.body: Town started with corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios, with a relationship more like you paying for a personal assistant, naturally filtering for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and have no time or energy. Muse is more like a middleman, shopper, or broker — although it has a paid subscription, the estimated main revenue source is still commission from matchmaking transactions, leaning toward mass users and blending into daily WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, cutting different scenarios and filtering out different users.

points.h: Bookmarks may be noise to an agent
points.body: The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was about extracting your favorite ingredients from Instagram saves, generating a shopping list, adjusting the menu by dinner party size and dietary restrictions, then completing shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, from a discovery platform into a decision and transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users complete transactions is absolutely not in the top scenarios users want to solve; users more want to solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in bookmarks; truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

points.h: GUI is a maze map for ordinary people
points.body: Today didn't initially want to make a standalone app, was very channel-heavy, integrated WeChat and Telegram, and completed most scenarios in channels. But it soon discovered the discoverability problem of features: users staring at a blank dialog box had no idea what to do. So it had to intervene with GUI, and doing GUI required a standalone app, and ultimately it still made chat in the app. Suki's takeaway is that GUI today no longer carries the user operation entry point like it used to, but is more like a map — to ordinary people, an agent is more like a maze hiding many treasures, and GUI is giving ordinary people a maze map, along which you can discover the treasures.

points.h: If 90% of effort goes to general capability, pivot
points.body: Suki originally worked on AI education product Monspeak, and during Spring Festival this year while making 2.0 discovered that to make a truly personalized teacher, 90% of the effort ended up going into how to make the agent run stably and have personalized memory. If 90% of the effort is on a very general capability, then conversely those general agents might casually finish and eat the vertical scenario. So judging that the C-end track ultimately won't leave that many players, that it will be highly concentrated with winner-take-all, Suki switched to joining a startup to build personal AI together.

points.h: This wave has no network effect to lock in users
points.body: Suki believes this AI transformation is very different from the last mobile internet wave: the biggest change this wave is technological innovation, not the narrative of scaling up, burning money to build network effects. There is no network effect or scale effect that can lock in users — as long as your product is good, I'll switch to another product the very next day, because no two-sided network platform has formed, and users have no need to stay with you. People stay on Xiaohongshu or Douyin because a two-sided network platform has formed, and it's impossible to easily migrate away. So innovative companies are actually easier to fight than in the last mobile internet wave — just hurry to innovate and win users with the best experience.

points.h: The most valuable thing is the middle processing layer
points.body: Finally, the question of where the most valuable position is in the personal agent era. Suki picks trust and habit — context is just the entry-level foundation, and ultimately it's the dependence, habit and trust formed through long-term use; if forced to choose, leaning more toward the end closer to the user, because model makers are still chasing each other, and the merchant and MCP end will naturally grow with the market. Mark thinks it's neither context nor the ecosystem layer: just getting a lot of context is completely insufficient, it doesn't directly deliver value, and memory is far more complex than imagined — something said last week may already be invalid this week, and if it stays in memory it's serious noise. The most valuable thing is the middle processing layer, a bit like Douyin's recommendation algorithm; how the execution mechanism works is each company's secret.

terms.def: AI that organizes context centered on the user themselves, understands them long-term, and proactively does things for them.
The engineering layer that wraps the model and is responsible for calling tools and completing tasks.
An open protocol ecosystem that lets AI call external tools and data.
The ability for AI to operate web pages through the browser interface on a person's behalf.
The general ability for AI to directly control the graphical interface to complete tasks.
The information AI can see about you, including history, preferences and the current task.
